tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Translate a continuous-time signal graph into a simplified unit step expression by identifying its breakpoints, interval formulas, and shifted unit-step windows.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Introduction to Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, a single nonzero interval from a to b, breakpoint markers at a and b, and the active interval highlighted clearly.

blocks.text: A graph is ready to convert when you can read its breakpoints first. The breakpoints tell you where the signal turns on, stays active, and turns off, so those times become the shifted step arguments in the expression.
For one finite interval, write a unit-step window as the difference of two shifted steps. The window is 1 on the active interval and 0 everywhere else, so it gates the signal to that segment only.

In the simplest pulse case, the active interval is $0 \le t < T$, so the same rule becomes $x(t)=A\big(u(t)-u(t-T)\big)$. This is the base pattern you will reuse whenever a graph has one nonzero interval.

For more complicated graphs, attach each interval formula to its own window, then combine the terms and simplify. The next steps will follow that same sequence: read the intervals, write each gated segment, and merge the result into one compact step expression.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Identifying Breakpoints and Interval Formulas from a Graph

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, alternating zero and nonzero flat pieces, breakpoint markers at -2, 0, 3, and 5, and segment labels 0, 2, -1, 3, 0 shown directly on the graph.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the displayed graph and write the ordered breakpoint list together with the interval formula table $\{(t_0,t_1]: f_1, (t_1,t_2]: f_2, \dots\}$.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the breakpoints in the graph. In this example, the signal changes at $t=-2$, $t=0$, $t=3$, and $t=5$, so those four times determine the ordered interval map.

Now assign one formula to each region between neighboring breakpoints. Here the graph is piecewise constant, so each interval keeps the height shown on the plot, and the breakpoint convention places each change point on the interval to its right.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(t)=0 \text{ for } t<-2,\; 2 \text{ for } -2\le t<0,\; -1 \text{ for } 0\le t<3,\; 3 \text{ for } 3\le t<5,\; 0 \text{ for } t\ge 5

explanation_blocks.text: That ordered breakpoint list and interval table are the complete input for the next conversion step. Keep the boundaries and interval values aligned exactly as shown, because the step-term rewrite will reuse this map directly.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Converting a Single Nonzero Graph Segment into a Step Window Term

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one isolated nonzero flat segment of height A on the interval from a to b, breakpoint markers at a and b, and zero elsewhere so the window-difference rule is visually obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the graph with $x(t)=A$ for $a\le t<b$ and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere into a step form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single nonzero interval with constant height $A$: the graph is zero before $a$, stays at $A$ on $a\le t<b$, and returns to zero after $b$. That means one window term is enough; the job is to gate the amplitude with the two breakpoints.
Use the standard window difference. $u(t-a)$ turns the signal on at $a$, and $u(t-b)$ turns it back off at $b$, so $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$ is 1 exactly on the active interval and 0 elsewhere.

Check the three regions in order. For $t<a$, both steps are 0. For $a\le t<b$, the first step is 1 and the second is 0. For $t\ge b$, both steps are 1, so the difference returns to 0. That verifies the exact single-window template for one isolated segment.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Constant Graph into Shifted Unit Steps

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at a, b, and c, a first plateau of height A on the interval from a to b, a second plateau of height B on the interval from b to c drawn below the time axis to emphasize signed levels, and zero elsewhere so the multi-window sum is visually obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the graph $0\to A\to B\to 0$ over two intervals to a unit-step sum.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a piecewise constant graph with two nonzero plateaus. Read the levels and breakpoints first: the signal is $A$ on $a\le t<b$, then $B$ on $b\le t<c$, and zero outside those intervals.

Write one shifted window for each plateau. The interval $a\le t<b$ is isolated by $u(t-a)-u(t-b)$, and the interval $b\le t<c$ is isolated by $u(t-b)-u(t-c)$; scaling each window by its plateau height gives the full signal.

Check the result interval by interval. Before $a$ both windows are off; on $a\le t<b$ only the first term contributes; on $b\le t<c$ only the second term contributes; after $c$ both terms are off again. The signs stay attached to the plateau heights, so the step sum matches the graph exactly.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Linear Graph into Windowed Segment Formulas

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one rising line segment from (0,0) to (2,2), one falling line segment from (2,2) to (4,0), breakpoint markers at 0, 2, and 4, and zero elsewhere so the two linear segment windows are visually obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the graph with $x(t)=t$ for $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=4-t$ for $2\le t<4$, and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere into a sum of windowed segment formulas.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is two linear pieces, not one constant plateau. Read each segment formula first: the signal rises like $t$ on $0\le t<2$ and falls like $4-t$ on $2\le t<4$. Then attach a gate that keeps each formula active only on its own interval.

Use one window per segment. The rising piece is kept on by $u(t)-u(t-2)$, and the falling piece is kept on by $u(t-2)-u(t-4)$. Multiplying each interval formula by its own window prevents the linear trend from extending past its breakpoints.

Check the intervals in order. Before $0$ both windows are off. On $0\le t<2$, only the rising segment remains. On $2\le t<4$, only the falling segment remains. After $4$, both windows are off again, so the windowed sum matches the graph on every interval.

sections.lesson_title: Converting Graphs into Unit Step Expressions
sections.section_title: Writing a Simplified Unit Step Expression from a Multi-Segment Graph

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at 0, 2, 4, and 6, a constant plateau at height 2 from 0 to 2, a falling line segment from (2,2) to (4,0), a constant plateau at height -1 from 4 to 6 drawn below the axis to emphasize the sign change, and zero elsewhere so the simplification across shared breakpoints is visually obvious.

example_content.example_prompt: Given the graph with $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=4-t$ for $2\le t<4$, $x(t)=-1$ for $4\le t<6$, and $x(t)=0$ elsewhere, derive and simplify one compact unit-step expression that matches all intervals.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a mixed graph with constant and linear pieces. Read the interval formulas first: the signal is $2$ on $0\le t<2$, then $4-t$ on $2\le t<4$, then $-1$ on $4\le t<6$, and $0$ elsewhere. The simplification comes from combining shared windows at the breakpoints.

Convert each segment independently. Use $u(t)-u(t-2)$ for the constant plateau, $u(t-2)-u(t-4)$ for the linear fall, and $u(t-4)-u(t-6)$ for the negative plateau. Then add the terms before simplifying the repeated breakpoint windows.
Now combine the shared breakpoint terms at $t=2$ and $t=4$. Collecting like step functions gives one compact expression with one coefficient per breakpoint, which is easier to read and check.

Check the intervals in order. Before $0$ every step is off. On $0\le t<2$ the value is $2$; on $2\le t<4$ it becomes $4-t$; on $4\le t<6$ it is $-1$; and after $6$ it returns to $0$. That confirms the simplified form matches the full graph exactly.

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph over t from -6 to 6. The signal is piecewise constant with breakpoint markers at $t=-3$, $t=-1$, $t=2$, and $t=4$. The signal value is 0 for $t<-3$, 1 on $-3\let<-1$, -2 on $-1\let<2$, 3 on $2\let<4$, and 0 for $t\ge4$. Show each plateau as a flat horizontal segment with clear breakpoint markers and small labels 0, 1, -2, 3, 0 directly on the corresponding regions. Axes labeled time and amplitude.

A clean continuous-time graph over t from -6 to 7. The signal is piecewise constant with breakpoint markers at $t=-4$, $t=-1$, $t=2$, and $t=5$. The signal value is 0 for $t<-4$, 2 on $-4\let<-1$, 0 on $-1\let<2$, -1 on $2\let<5$, and 0 for $t\ge5$. Show the zero-valued middle interval explicitly and label the plateaus 0, 2, 0, -1, 0 directly on the graph. Axes labeled time and amplitude.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph below. Which ordered breakpoint list and interval formulas match it?

choice_blocks.text: Breakpoints $-3,-1,2,4$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-3$, $1$ for $-3\le t<-1$, $-2$ for $-1\le t<2$, $3$ for $2\le t<4$, and $0$ for $t\ge 4$.
Breakpoints $-3,-1,2,4$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-3$, $-2$ for $-3\le t<-1$, $1$ for $-1\le t<2$, $3$ for $2\le t<4$, and $0$ for $t\ge 4$.
Breakpoints $-3,-1,4$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-3$, $1$ for $-3\le t<-1$, $3$ for $-1\le t<4$, and $0$ for $t\ge 4$.
Breakpoints $1,2,3,4$; intervals: $0$ for $t<1$, $1$ for $1\le t<2$, $-2$ for $2\le t<3$, $3$ for $3\le t<4$, and $0$ for $t\ge 4$.
Breakpoints $-3,-1,2,4$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-3$, $1$ for $-3<t\le -1$, $-2$ for $-1<t\le 2$, $3$ for $2<t\le 4$, and $0$ for $t>4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the breakpoints from left to right and keep the interval values attached to the regions between them. The graph changes at $t=-3,-1,2,4$, so there are five intervals, including the leading and trailing zero regions.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph below. Which ordered breakpoint list and interval formulas match it?

choice_blocks.text: Breakpoints $-4,-1,2,5$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-4$, $2$ for $-4\le t<-1$, $0$ for $-1\le t<2$, $-1$ for $2\le t<5$, and $0$ for $t\ge 5$.
Breakpoints $-4,-1,2,5$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-4$, $2$ for $-4\le t<2$, $-1$ for $2\le t<5$, and $0$ for $t\ge 5$.
Breakpoints $-4,-1,5$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-4$, $2$ for $-4\le t<-1$, $-1$ for $-1\le t<5$, and $0$ for $t\ge 5$.
Breakpoints $1,4,6,9$; intervals: $0$ for $t<1$, $2$ for $1\le t<4$, $0$ for $4\le t<6$, $-1$ for $6\le t<9$, and $0$ for $t\ge 9$.
Breakpoints $-4,-1,2,5$; intervals: $0$ for $t<-4$, $2$ for $-4<t\le -1$, $0$ for $-1<t\le 2$, $-1$ for $2<t\le 5$, and $0$ for $t>5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The middle interval is zero, but it still has its own breakpoints and must stay in the ordered list. Read every change point in increasing time order, then assign the level on each interval without collapsing the zero region.

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one isolated flat nonzero segment of height 4 on the interval from -2 to 1, breakpoint markers at -2 and 1, and zero elsewhere.
A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one isolated flat nonzero segment of height -3 on the interval from 0 to 5, breakpoint markers at 0 and 5, and zero elsewhere.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, select the correct single-window conversion expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph is $4$ on the interval from $-2$ to $1$ and zero elsewhere, so the gate is $u(t+2)-u(t-1)$. Multiplying by the amplitude gives $4(u(t+2)-u(t-1))$.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, select the correct single-window conversion expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph is $-3$ on the interval from $0$ to $5$ and zero elsewhere, so the gate is $u(t)-u(t-5)$. Multiplying by the amplitude gives $-3(u(t)-u(t-5))$.

sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Constant Graph into Shifted Unit Steps

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at 1, 3, 5, and 7, a constant plateau of height 2 from 1 to 3, a constant plateau of height -1 from 3 to 5 drawn below the axis to emphasize the negative level, a constant plateau of height 3 from 5 to 7, and zero elsewhere so the three-window sum is visually obvious.

A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at -1, 2, and 5, a constant plateau of height -2 from -1 to 2 drawn below the axis, a constant plateau of height 1 from 2 to 5, and zero elsewhere so the two-window sum is visually obvious.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the unit-step expression that matches the graph below.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the breakpoints first: the graph is 2 from 1 to 3, -1 from 3 to 5, and 3 from 5 to 7. That means one shifted window per plateau, with the plateau height attached to each window.
The other choices either merge intervals, flip the negative plateau, reverse a window order, or collapse the whole graph into one wide window. The correct sum keeps each plateau on its own interval.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the unit-step expression that matches the graph below.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph is -2 from -1 to 2 and 1 from 2 to 5, so the first window is $u(t+1)$-$u(t-2)$ and the second window is $u(t-2)$-$u(t-5)$. Attach the plateau height to each window.

The wrong answers either stretch a plateau across too much time, flip the sign on the first level, reverse the step order, or drop the second plateau entirely. The correct expression matches both constant sections exactly.

sections.section_title: Converting a Piecewise Linear Graph into Windowed Segment Formulas

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one rising line segment from (-1,0) to (1,2), one falling line segment from (1,2) to (3,0), breakpoint markers at -1, 1, and 3, and zero elsewhere so the two linear segment windows are visually obvious.

A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, one rising line segment from (0,0) to (3,3), one falling line segment from (3,3) to (6,0), breakpoint markers at 0, 3, and 6, and zero elsewhere so the two linear segment windows are visually obvious.

prompt_blocks.text: Select the windowed expression that matches the graph.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read each linear segment and gate it to its own interval. The rising piece is $t+1$ on $-1\le t<1$, and the falling piece is $3-t$ on $1\le t<3$, so each piece needs its own shifted-unit-step window.
Choices that drop a window, flip the sign on the falling ramp, or shift the breakpoints do not match the graph on both segments.

prompt_blocks.text: Select the windowed expression that matches the graph.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph rises as $t$ on $0\le t<3$ and falls as $6-t$ on $3\le t<6$, so the correct expression uses one window for each interval with matching start and stop times.
The wrong choices either keep the falling ramp with the wrong sign, reverse the window order, move the breakpoints, or change the rise magnitude.

image_slots.image_description: A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at 0, 2, 4, and 6, a constant plateau at height 3 from 0 to 2, a falling line segment from (2,3) to (4,1), a constant plateau at height -2 from 4 to 6 drawn below the axis, and zero elsewhere. A clean continuous-time graph with a labeled time axis, breakpoint markers at -1, 1, 3, and 5, a constant plateau at height -2 from -1 to 1, a rising line segment from (1,0) to (3,2), a constant plateau at height 1 from 3 to 5, and zero elsewhere. Keep the same simple line style and breakpoint labeling used in the lesson examples.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the most simplified unit-step expression equivalent to the graph.
Select the expression that matches all intervals after the breakpoint terms are combined.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write one windowed term for each segment, then combine the shared breakpoint terms at $t=2$ and $t=4$. The simplified result is the only choice that keeps the plateau at 3, the linear segment $5-t$, and the final plateau at $-2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the most simplified unit-step expression equivalent to the graph.
Pick the expression that matches the negative interval, the rising ramp, the positive plateau, and the return to zero.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph has one negative plateau, one linear rise, one positive plateau, and then it returns to zero. Combine the window terms so the breakpoint contributions collapse into a single simplified expression.
